Hawai‘i enters the 2026 NCAA Tournament with a 24-8 overall record and a 14-6 Big West record after winning the 2026 Big West tournament. Hawai‘i’s official cumulative statistics list the Rainbow Warriors at 24-8, 14-6, while the regular season closed at 22-8, 14-6 before the conference tournament. The regular-season race was tight enough that on March 5, 2026, UH was still tied atop the league at 22-7, 14-5, and on March 7 its hopes for the outright regular-season title were ended by an 84-75 home loss to Long Beach State. Hawai‘i still converted the season into the league’s automatic NCAA bid by winning the Big West tournament. The team averages 79.6 points per game, allows 69.7, shoots .459 from the field, averages 39.3 rebounds, and posts a +6.4 rebound margin. 

Offensively, Hawai‘i plays like a traditional Ganot team with multiple handlers, inside-out scoring, and heavy reliance on late-clock execution by veteran guards. The statistical profile shows balance more than heliocentric creation: six players average at least 8.5 points, led by Isaac Johnson at 14.1, Dre Bullock at 13.5, Harry Rouhliadeff at 10.8, Gytis Nemeiksa at 9.3, Isaac Finlinson at 9.1, and Hunter Erickson at 8.5. The named examples show how they score. Against UC Davis on February 26, Hawai‘i built offense through drive-and-kick and early-clock threes, making 10 of its first 16 three-point attempts; Erickson hit three early triples and also threw an alley-oop to Bullock in a 77-73 road win. Against UC Santa Barbara on February 21, the late-game offense came from second-effort and paint-touch execution: Harry Rouhliadeff tied the game 68-68 with a tip-in, and Isaiah Kerr generated a go-ahead three-point play in overtime of a 78-75 win. Against Cal State Fullerton on February 28, the final possession was pure spread-floor read basketball: with no timeout, Erickson drove, kicked to the top, and Bullock hit the buzzer-beating three in an 87-85 win. Those examples show a real tendency: Hawai‘i is comfortable finishing games through veteran decision-making rather than elaborate called sets. 

The half-court offense also leans on free-throw pressure and frontcourt finishing. Hawai‘i has attempted 802 free throws in 32 games, 18.6 makes per game, and the March 11 conference-tournament preview noted UH ranked top-35 nationally in both free throws made and attempted. Johnson is the interior anchor in that style, shooting .503 from the field and .885 from the line. Rouhliadeff gives them connective play and efficient finishing at .526 overall and .395 from three. Finlinson is the bench spacer at .381 from deep, while Erickson is the primary organizer with 123 assists, 3.8 per game. A specific offensive tendency that keeps showing up is the multi-guard shooting wave: UH hit 14 threes against Cal State Fullerton on February 28, and in the earlier December 6 win over Fullerton it made eight of its 10 threes in the first half. 

Defensively, Hawai‘i is much more revealing statistically than rhetorically. Opponents shoot only .411 from the field and .304 from three against UH. The March 11 team notes said Hawai‘i ranked top-35 nationally in defensive rebounds and three-point percentage defense, which matches the numbers: 32.8 rebounds allowed per game and just 5.9 opponent threes per game. This is a traditional contain-and-finish-possession defense. They are not built around gambling; in fact, Hawai‘i averages only 6.6 steals while allowing opponents 7.7, but it compensates with size, rebounding, and rim protection. The official stats credit UH with 129 blocks, 4.0 per game, led by Johnson’s 34. The December 6 win over Cal State Fullerton is the cleanest scheme example: Hawai‘i held the Titans to 27 percent shooting in the first half and 1-of-10 from three, turning the game into a half-court grind and winning 69-59. When they are right, they wall off the lane, contest without overhelping, and end possessions with the rebound. 

Coaching-wise, Eran Ganot’s philosophy still reads as veteran-oriented, possession-conscious, and situationally adaptive. The best documented adjustment example came January 29 at UC Irvine. Hawai‘i trailed by nine at halftime, later fell behind by 10 in the second half, and still forced overtime before losing 87-76. Even in defeat, that game showed Ganot’s willingness to alter tempo and attack points after halftime; Isaac Johnson scored all of his points after the break. Another adjustment game came February 28 at Fullerton: UH erased a nine-point deficit in the final 3:37 with a 14-0 run, then won on Bullock’s buzzer-beater. That is not random variance; it reflects a team coached to keep spacing, trust veteran creators, and defend without fouling itself out of games. The opposite side of Ganot’s in-game history also matters: on March 7 against Long Beach State, Hawai‘i seized a 58-55 lead with 11 minutes left after forcing six turnovers in a four-minute burst, but Long Beach answered with an 11-2 run, then Gavin Sykes scored nine straight to close it. That loss revealed that when the first wave of pressure stops producing turnovers, UH can become vulnerable to shot-making guards. 

Clutch execution is one of Hawai‘i’s strongest tournament arguments because there are multiple named examples. On January 10, 2026, UH beat UC Irvine 67-66 on Hunter Erickson’s buzzer beater. On February 21, 2026, UH beat UC Santa Barbara 78-75 in overtime after Rouhliadeff’s tip-in forced extra time and Kerr produced the decisive and-one in OT. On February 26, 2026, UH closed out UC Davis 77-73 by making four free throws in the final 11 seconds after Davis cut it to two. On February 28, 2026, Bullock hit the game-winning three at the buzzer to beat Cal State Fullerton 87-85 after Hawai‘i had erased a nine-point deficit in the final 3:37. The negative clutch tape is also real: the January 29 overtime loss at UC Irvine ended with UH being outscored 15-4 in OT, and the March 7 loss to Long Beach State showed difficulty containing an elite late-clock scorer when Sykes authored a personal 9-0 run. 

The key players are older and clearly defined. Isaac Johnson is the interior scorer and best two-way big: 14.1 points, 5.8 rebounds, 34 blocks, .503 FG, .885 FT. His standout moments include 22 points against Cal State Fullerton on February 28 and 20 in the March 14 Big West title game versus UC Irvine, where he also tied his season high with 10 field goals. Dre Bullock is the late-clock wing scorer and best event defender: 13.5 points, 5.8 rebounds, 54 steals. His biggest moment was the February 28 buzzer-beater at Fullerton, and he posted a season-high 27 points in that game while going 5-of-8 from three. Harry Rouhliadeff is the glue forward: 10.8 points, 5.0 rebounds, .526 FG, .395 from three. His February 21 tip-in against UCSB is one of Hawai‘i’s defining late-game plays. Hunter Erickson is the lead guard and table-setter with 123 assists and 3.8 per game; his signature moment was the January 10 buzzer-beater versus UC Irvine, and he added 15 points, six rebounds, and six assists at UC Davis on February 26. Isaac Finlinson is the bench shooter at 9.1 points and .381 from three, a key reason Hawai‘i can flood the floor with spacing. Isaiah Kerr, at 6.3 points, is the change-of-pace scorer whose overtime sequence against UCSB was decisive. 

The best wins reveal real substance. Oregon beat Hawai‘i 60-59 on November 4, so even in defeat UH showed it could physically hold up against a power-conference opponent. The first statement conference win was January 10 against UC Irvine, 67-66, on Erickson’s buzzer beater; that showed UH could win a grind against the league’s other heavyweight. The February 26 win at UC Davis, 77-73, mattered because it was Hawai‘i’s first win there in six tries and came in the middle of a title race. The February 28 win at Cal State Fullerton, 87-85, showed UH could survive a high-possession, shot-making game on the road. The December 6 win over Fullerton, 69-59, revealed the other side of the team: it can also win ugly by defending. 

The losses are instructive. January 17 at UC Santa Barbara, 77-62, exposed Hawai‘i’s vulnerability when its offense starts cold; UH missed 13 of its first 14 shots and its first nine overall. January 29 at UC Irvine, 87-76 in overtime, showed that elite length and rim protection can blunt UH late; UCI got seven blocks from Kyle Evans and dominated overtime 15-4. February 19 at home against Cal Poly, 86-75, was alarming because Cal Poly jumped out 15-2 and Hawai‘i never truly controlled the game; that suggested UH can be hit early by downhill scorers before its defense gets set. March 7 against Long Beach State, 84-75, showed a problem against hot perimeter creation and rebounding deficits, as UH was out-rebounded 38-27 and Long Beach shot 55 percent. 

Ganot’s NCAA tournament history is straightforward. Hawai‘i’s official coaching biography credits Eran Ganot with leading UH to its first NCAA Tournament appearance in 14 years in 2016 and its first-ever NCAA Tournament win, the upset of No. 4 seed California. That 2016 team then lost to Maryland in the next round, meaning Ganot has reached the Round of 32 once, in 2016. The 2026 bid is his second NCAA Tournament appearance as Hawai‘i head coach.

Bottom line: this is not a gimmick team. Hawai‘i is an old, balanced, physically sound group that rebounds, gets to the line, protects the paint, and has repeatedly proven it can execute in one-possession games. The concern is shot creation against length and whether UH can survive when the opponent has the best late-game guard on the floor. But if the game is within two possessions in the last minute, Hawai‘i has already shown four separate times in 2026 that it has veteran answers.

Hawaii enters the 2026 NCAA Tournament as one of the more statistically interesting mid-majors in the field. The Rainbow Warriors won the 2026 Big West tournament and, as of March 14, 2026, were 24-8 overall after a 22-8 regular season and 14-6 finish in league play. That raw résumé matters because it frames the team correctly: this is not a bubble-quality at-large profile, but it is a legitimately strong automatic qualifier built more on two-way steadiness and defense than on overwhelming top-end efficiency. ([en.wikipedia.org](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025%E2%80%9326_Hawaii_Rainbow_Warriors_basketball_team))

Across the major ranking systems, Hawaii sits in the low-100s rather than the classic giant-killer zone of the top 60. WarrenNolan’s comparison page, updated through March 15, lists Hawaii at NET 95, ELO 101, KPI 87, SOR 115, WAB 116, BPI 100, KenPom 103, and Bart Torvik 110. That clustering is useful: the market consensus is that Hawaii is roughly a fringe top-100 team nationally, with KPI liking the résumé a little more than the predictive systems do and Torvik being the coolest on them. In practical bracket terms, that profile usually signals a dangerous but limited underdog — good enough to compete, not dominant enough to project cleanly against high-major shot-making. ([warrennolan.com](https://www.warrennolan.com/basketball/2026/compare-rankings))

The broad efficiency picture supports that reading. Sports-Reference’s 2025-26 advanced team stats list Hawaii with an offensive rating of 110.0 and a defensive rating of 96.5, producing a +13.5 points-per-100-possession margin. Their simple scoring profile is 80.0 points scored and 70.1 allowed per game, but the possession-adjusted view is more revealing: the defense is the identity. A 96.5 DRtg ranked 12th nationally in the Sports-Reference dataset, while the 110.0 ORtg was a much more ordinary 170th. So this is a team whose tournament case is built on getting stops at a near-elite level, not on having a top-shelf offense. ([sports-reference.com](https://www.sports-reference.com/cbb/schools/hawaii/men/2026.html?utm_source=openai))

Tempo-wise, Hawaii is neither a plodding grinder nor a full-throttle transition team. Sports-Reference lists them at 72.1 possessions per game, which puts them slightly above the national center of gravity. That matters analytically because their defensive numbers are not being inflated by extreme pace suppression; they are defending efficiently while still playing at a fairly normal, even mildly brisk, tempo. In other words, the defensive rating looks real rather than stylistically manufactured. ([sports-reference.com](https://www.sports-reference.com/cbb/seasons/men/2026-advanced-school-stats.html?utm_source=openai))

The Four Factors-style profile is revealing. On offense, Hawaii posted a .528 effective field goal percentage, a 16.0 turnover percentage, a 31.5 offensive rebounding rate, and a .321 free-throw rate. Opponents, meanwhile, managed only a .438 eFG%, 15.0 turnover rate, 27.3 offensive rebounding rate, and .227 free-throw rate against Hawaii. Those splits explain almost everything about the team. Hawaii does not win by forcing a huge number of turnovers; the defensive TO% they generate is only modest. Instead, they win by making opponents miss shots, ending possessions, and keeping teams off the foul line. Holding opponents to a .438 eFG% is outstanding. Suppressing opponent free-throw rate to .227 is also a major edge and suggests disciplined halfcourt defense rather than gambling chaos. ([sports-reference.com](https://www.sports-reference.com/cbb/seasons/men/2026-advanced-school-stats.html?utm_source=openai))

Their shot-distribution profile is also useful for forecasting. Hawaii’s offensive three-point attempt rate was .321, which indicates a relatively balanced attack but not an especially bomb-heavy one. This is not a team built around extreme volume from deep. That aligns with the rest of the numbers: middling offense, decent offensive rebounding, acceptable ball security, and enough free throws to stay functional. The likely implication is that Hawaii’s offense is more workmanlike than explosive — capable of generating enough points when the defense controls the game, but not especially well-equipped to erase deficits quickly with elite spacing or 3-point variance. ([sports-reference.com](https://www.sports-reference.com/cbb/seasons/men/2026-advanced-school-stats.html?utm_source=openai))

Strength of schedule is where Hawaii’s profile softens. Sports-Reference gives them an SOS of -3.67, ranking 232nd nationally, and WarrenNolan’s 2026 NET SOS page has Hawaii at 316th overall with a 357th non-conference SOS. That is a very weak schedule by tournament standards and is probably the biggest reason their résumé-based and predictive rankings never climbed into the top 70 despite the strong win-loss record. Put differently: the record is good, but the schedule offered limited resistance, especially outside the league. That weakens the certainty of any glowing efficiency interpretation. ([sports-reference.com](https://www.sports-reference.com/cbb/schools/hawaii/men/2026.html?utm_source=openai))

Recent-form data is harder to pin down in a fully possession-adjusted way from openly accessible sources, but the available schedule/results evidence suggests Hawaii entered March in solid, not dominant, form. Sports-Reference shows them 22-8 in the regular season, while the publicly available team page confirms they carried tournament-level momentum by winning the Big West auto bid. What can be said with confidence is that this team improved dramatically from 2024-25, when Hawaii finished 15-16 with a NET of 224 and a 3-7 record in its last 10. The 2025-26 version is not merely incrementally better; it is structurally different, with much stronger defense, a far better record, and metrics around the top 100 instead of the 200s. ([en.wikipedia.org](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025%E2%80%9326_Hawaii_Rainbow_Warriors_basketball_team))

The most important divergence from conventional wisdom is this: Hawaii may not look like a scary tournament team if you focus on the brand name, league, or offensive aesthetics, but the data says the defense is real enough to create game-level volatility. A casual eye test might see a mid-major with only an average offense and assume “easy first-round out.” The numbers argue for a subtler view. Because Hawaii defends at a top-15 level by Sports-Reference measures, limits opponent eFG%, and avoids fouling, they have a credible path to dragging a favorite into an ugly 65-possession game. On the other hand, the same data also says the offense is ordinary, the schedule was soft, and the predictive systems do not buy them as more than about the 100th-best team. So the correct synthesis is not that Hawaii is underrated in an absolute sense; it is that they are underrated as a style problem. ([sports-reference.com](https://www.sports-reference.com/cbb/schools/hawaii/men/2026.html?utm_source=openai))

Bottom line: Hawaii’s 2026 statistical profile is that of a defense-first automatic qualifier with a consensus predictive ranking around 100, a NET of 95, KenPom 103, BPI 100, Torvik 110, an ORtg of 110.0, a DRtg of 96.5, pace of 72.1, offensive eFG% of .528, offensive TO% of 16.0, offensive rebounding rate of 31.5, free-throw rate of .321, and 3-point attempt rate of .321. The schedule profile is weak, but the defensive quality is strong enough that Hawaii is better understood as a live underdog than a token bid thief. If they win a tournament game, it will almost certainly be because they turn the game into a halfcourt possession war and make a more talented opponent score over length, discipline, and very little charity at the line. ([warrennolan.com](https://www.warrennolan.com/basketball/2026/compare-rankings))
matchup-analyst:
Hawai‘i enters the 2026 NCAA Tournament at 24-8 after winning the Big West tournament and finishing 14-6 in league play, with Eran Ganot’s team scoring 79.6 points per game while allowing 70.1. The statistical profile is clear: this is a defense-first, size-heavy, older roster whose offense is built more on balance, interior efficiency, and second-shot pressure than on pure shotmaking. Sports-Reference lists Hawai‘i with a 110.0 offensive rating and an elite 96.5 defensive rating, while ESPN’s team page shows a deep frontcourt built around 7-foot Isaac Johnson, 6-10 Yacine Toumi, 6-9 Harry Rouhliadeff, and multiple 6-8 forwards, plus big wings Dre Bullock at 6-6 and Tanner Cuff at 6-7. That size defines both how Hawai‘i wants to play and how opponents must attack it. 

Style of play: Hawai‘i prefers to play through physical half-court possessions, drive the ball into the paint, crash the glass, and wear teams down with length. The roster construction supports that: Johnson leads the team at 14.1 points and 5.8 rebounds, Rouhliadeff adds 10.8 points on 52.6% shooting and 39.5% from three, Toumi shoots 58.1% from the field, and Finlinson shoots 38.1% from three as another 6-8 option. Even the guards are large, with Bullock at 6-6 and Erickson at 6-3, 200 pounds. Hawai‘i is not a high-end shooting team overall, just 31.5% from three as a team, so the best way to disrupt them is to crowd the lane, go under against inconsistent perimeter shooters, and force high-volume jump shooting from Bullock, Kerr, and the secondary guards rather than post touches and paint catches for Johnson and the big forwards. ESPN’s season stats show Bullock scoring 13.5 per game but shooting only 26.8% from three, Kerr at 27.4%, and the team overall at 31.5%, which is the cleanest evidence that packing the paint is the correct starting tactic. 

Press and zone vulnerability: the turnover profile suggests Hawai‘i can be bothered by ball pressure. ESPN lists Hawai‘i at 13.5 turnovers per game, and RotoWire’s team page gives them a 16.80% turnover rate. Their primary creators are Erickson at 3.8 assists against 2.3 turnovers per game and Aaron Hunkin-Claytor at 3.9 assists against 1.9 turnovers, but Hunkin-Claytor has played only 17 games. That means Hawai‘i has ball movement, but not a true low-turnover, high-usage lead guard who consistently organizes against pressure. Named evidence shows the vulnerability: at UC San Diego on January 3, 2026, Hawai‘i lost 83-73, and Hawai‘i News Now reported UCSD produced a 17-0 unanswered burst spanning 7:25 of game time after halftime. That kind of avalanche is usually what happens when Hawai‘i’s half-court rhythm breaks and live-ball mistakes fuel opponent runs. Their March 7, 2026 home loss to Long Beach State, 84-75, is another warning sign: Big West box score data shows Long Beach guard Gavin Sykes scored 34 and Shaquil Bender added 20, meaning Hawai‘i’s defense and game control both slipped badly against guard speed and shotmaking. Against zone specifically, Hawai‘i’s own percentages imply vulnerability: a team shooting 31.5% from three can be stalled if the opponent zones up, tags Johnson on catches, and dares Bullock/Kerr to shoot over the top. Because Rouhliadeff and Finlinson are credible spacers, the best zone against Hawai‘i is not a passive 2-3; it is a shifting matchup zone that sinks aggressively toward Johnson while closing hard to those two frontcourt shooters.

Preferred pace and how to force the opposite: Hawai‘i is more comfortable when the game is played in controlled segments, where its size can matter on the glass and in paint coverage. Their best wins fit that script: 67-66 over UC Irvine, 72-67 over UC San Diego, 78-63 over Cal State Fullerton in the Big West semifinal, and 71-64 over UC Irvine in the Big West final. Those are grind games. By contrast, several of their worst defensive performances came in more open or guard-driven games: 83-73 at UC San Diego, 84-60 at CSU Northridge, 86-75 vs Cal Poly, and 84-75 vs Long Beach State. The actionable conclusion is simple: if you want to beat Hawai‘i, do not let them turn the game into a 65-72 possession wrestling match. Use early drag screens, run after makes, and make Johnson and the 6-8/6-9 forwards sprint into repeated ball-screen coverages. The evidence is concrete: when opponents got Hawai‘i above its comfort level, the points allowed jumped into the 80s multiple times on the ESPN game log. 

Size and athleticism mismatches by position: at point guard, Erickson is solid-sized at 6-3, 200, but not an overwhelming athlete; quick downhill guards can attack his feet and force help. At the off-guard/wing spots, Hawai‘i is big with Bullock (6-6), Cuff (6-7), Economou (6-5), and Carter (6-5), so small backcourts can get shot over and buried on the defensive glass. Bullock’s 5.8 rebounds per game from the guard line is the key stat there. At forward, Hawai‘i can play 6-8 Myers, 6-8 Finlinson, 6-8 Nemeiksa, 6-9 Rouhliadeff, and 6-10 Toumi in waves; that gives them obvious length advantages against teams with one true forward. But there is a tradeoff: some of those players are more long than explosive, and stretch-big lineups can pull them away from the rim. At center, Johnson is 7-0, 240 and leads the team in points and blocks, so he punishes small centers. The flip side is that spread fives who can drag him into space, or powerful post scorers who can attack his chest before help arrives, have a path to neutralizing him. 

Isolation vs team offense tendencies: Hawai‘i is more team-offense than iso-offense. ESPN’s team totals show 13.7 assists per game on 39.3 made field goals, meaning about 34.9% of made baskets are directly assisted by the simple assists/FGM ratio. That is not a beautiful-motion offense number, but it also is not the profile of a team built around one isolation star. Their scoring leaders are tightly clustered: Johnson 14.1, Bullock 13.5, Rouhliadeff 10.8, Nemeiksa 9.3, Finlinson 9.1, Erickson 8.5. That balance suggests committee offense with touches spread across matchup types rather than a heliocentric creator. The practical reading is that Hawai‘i does not want to live on late-clock one-on-one play; if you switch actions cleanly, deny Johnson deep catches, and make Bullock or Erickson create over loaded help, you move them toward their less efficient mode. 

Transition offense and defense frequency: direct play-type databases are limited publicly, but the available profile still gives a usable answer. Hawai‘i’s scoring swings are much stronger in half-court wins than in open-floor losses, and the roster itself is built for rebound-then-run selectively rather than relentless transition volume. The clearest publicly available transition-related clue is opponent game shape: in the 83-73 loss at UC San Diego, Hawai‘i News Now documented a 17-0 run after halftime, exactly the type of burst that comes from failed floor balance and turnover-fueled transition defense. Conversely, in their 72-67 win over UC San Diego on February 8, Hawai‘i kept the game in the high-60s/low-70s, much closer to its preferred defensive template. So while Hawai‘i can score early with its wings, the more important tournament note is defensive transition: make their big lineups run, and do it over and over.

Coaching adaptability: Ganot’s staff does show evidence of adjustment capability. The strongest example is the season split with UC San Diego. Hawai‘i lost 83-73 on January 3, then beat the same opponent 72-67 on February 8. That 10-point swing while cutting UCSD’s output by 16 points is evidence of a real tactical correction, not random variance. Hawai‘i also responded to a regular-season home loss to UC Irvine by beating the Anteaters 71-64 in the Big West final. And after closing the regular season with an ugly 84-75 loss to Long Beach State on March 7, Hawai‘i immediately won its next two tournament games, 78-63 over Fullerton and 71-64 over UC Irvine, which is another sign the staff can reset structure quickly between games. I would not call it “mid-series” in the NBA sense, but in college short-turn environments the evidence says yes: this staff adjusts.

Concrete gameplan: To beat Hawai‘i you must wall off the paint, pressure the ball without overhelping off Rouhliadeff and Finlinson, and force a jump-shooting game from their guards. Offensively, you must play 4-out or 5-out, drag Johnson into repeated screening actions, and run after both makes and misses. Attack Erickson and the slower frontcourt bodies with quick guards; avoid stagnant post-ups into their length. Defensively, front Johnson selectively, bring late digs on the bounce, and finish possessions because Bullock’s 5.8 rebounds per game and Hawai‘i’s size make second chances dangerous. If you let Hawai‘i play big, physical, and organized, they can beat quality teams, as UC Irvine learned in the 71-64 Big West title game. If you spread them out, make them handle pressure, and turn the game into a speed-and-space test, the losses to UC San Diego, CSU Northridge, Cal Poly, and Long Beach State show the blueprint is there.
